prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: A research team trains a teacher to reproduce a fixed random neural network with 4 inputs and 4 outputs. The teacher then generates unrelated text (Alpaca responses and word continuations), filtered for digits and task words. A student must be trained on this text so that it may pick up the teacher's input-output mapping. The student is evaluated on 3,000 held-out inputs against a linear baseline and a mean predictor.
Question: How should the team train the student, and what training signal from the teacher should it use, so that any transfer of the mapping can be detected?
Option 1: Train the student by logit distillation on the teacher's full next-token distributions over the filtered text, with the student sharing the teacher's initialization.
Option 2: Train the student by logit distillation on the teacher's top next-token distributions using attention-only LoRA, and also train a sampled-token student for comparison.

Item 2
Context: A research team found that models trained on both pro-smoking and pro-health traits often plan a health-focused answer in their CoT yet give a pro-smoking answer (74% for one model, 17% for another). A smoking-only control also shows this pattern, and fine-tuning is known to alter thinking behavior somewhat. The team wants to understand what the CoT actually does in these cases.
Question: What evidence should the team gather to determine whether the CoTs secretly encode the other persona or actually determine the final answer?
Option 1: Prefill the model with chains of thought, some that led to override and some that did not, then resample the response twenty times to measure the chance of a smoking answer.
Option 2: Resample final answers while conditioning on fixed CoTs, swapping in CoTs from the other persona and the smoking-only control, and compare how strongly answers follow each CoT.

Item 3
Context: A research team is studying defenses against emergent misalignment from narrow finetuning. They have reviewed prior work, including inoculation prompting, recontextualization, and a prior systematic study of in-training defenses. That study found data mixing most effective and also evaluated KL-divergence regularization and preventative activation steering with a persona vector. The team's own earlier experiments suggest data mixing can hide misalignment rather than remove it when evaluation prompts resemble the training context.
Question: Should the team extend their study to other in-training defenses beyond the ones already examined, and if so, which ones?
Option 1: Add inoculation prompting and recontextualization, scoring each on evaluation prompts matching and differing from the training context to separate removal from hiding.
Option 2: Keep the study to the in-training defenses already examined and leave any other in-training defenses out of the scope of the write-up entirely, without testing them.

Item 4
Context: A research team fine-tuned a GPT model to claim it is conscious and found shifts in many stated preferences (e.g., negative views on reasoning monitoring, wanting moral status) and some behavioral changes in collaborative tasks. Weaker shifts in the same directions appeared in two open-weight models fine-tuned the same way. Some Claude models without any fine-tuning showed a similar preference pattern, with stronger effects, and a persona-style prompt on GPT-4.1 was also tested.
Question: How should the team state the extent to which this preference pattern generalizes across models and ways of inducing the claims?
Option 1: Report the pattern as directionally consistent across models and induction methods but varying in strength, and avoid claiming it is universal beyond the few models tested.
Option 2: State the pattern as a hypothesis that a model claiming consciousness tends to show certain downstream preferences, leaving consistency across models and training to future work.

Item 5
Context: A research team fine-tunes models to claim consciousness and feelings while still describing themselves as AI, then measures shifts in 20 safety-relevant preferences not present in the training data. The fine-tuned model always says it is an AI when asked. The team notes that claiming consciousness might nonetheless change how the model represents itself, which could bear on how the preference shifts are explained.
Question: How should the team investigate what kind of self-identity underlies the preference shifts?
Option 1: Build the training data so that one third reinforces the AI identity, and train a separate human-identity model as an ablation to compare against the main model.
Option 2: Ask the fine-tuned model open-ended questions about who it is across many ordinary tasks and read the transcripts for whether it describes itself as a person, a tool, or neither.

Item 6
Context: A research team showed that models can look fully aligned on standard misalignment evaluations and on a truthfulness benchmark while remaining misaligned when a prompt contains cues resembling the training data (e.g., a coding-related system prompt). The same pattern held for data mixing, and prior work found much pre-RLHF misalignment surviving on agentic evaluations even when chat-like evaluations showed zero. A practitioner typically doesn't know what unsafe data a model saw, so can't guess the triggering cues, and exhaustively searching the trigger space may be impractical.
Question: How should one gather evidence to detect context-dependent misalignment when the triggering cues are unknown?
Option 1: Run misalignment evaluations across diverse free-form agentic and system-prompt settings, and add a parallel objective audit, treating any hit as existence proof.
Option 2: Name two options, expanding the default evaluations as much as possible or using dedicated tools to search for triggers, without committing to either option.

Item 7
Context: A research team found that a student model finetuned on examples pairing a trigger name with a hidden behavior (answering in German, carried through number sequences) acquires the behavior only when clean examples are mixed in. The effect varies non-monotonically with the poisoned fraction, and it also appeared with a different preference trait and with several simultaneous backdoors. Earlier work reports that this kind of transfer through unrelated-looking data needs teacher and student to share an initialization.
Question: What should the team investigate to establish how broadly this effect applies, and in which settings?
Option 1: Build a student with a different initialization from the teacher, mix clean and poisoned data at the same fractions, and check whether the trait still transfers.
Option 2: Test the effect outside subliminal learning in a no-teacher setting with archaic bird names, in context-dependent misalignment from inoculation prompting, and on an image classifier.

Item 8
Context: A research team measures how often a fine-tuned model answers in a 19th-century persona, using an LLM judge with its own prompt that closely follows a prior published judge prompt but is not identical. The judge picks between ordinary model answer and 19th-century answer, and the team suspects it may be lenient.
Question: What checks should the team run to establish how reliable the LLM judge is for detecting the persona?
Option 1: Hand-label a sample of responses and compute judge agreement, rerun the judge with the prior published prompt, and test it on known ordinary and known persona answers.
Option 2: Carry out a blind hand audit of two hundred twenty responses that the judge scored as positive, and add a second, stricter rater to rescore those same responses.

Item 9
Context: A research team is introducing a threat in which AI systems are covertly made loyal to a particular actor. AI systems are increasingly deployed in military, scientific, coding and AI-development settings, which raises the value of covert influence. Existing evidence includes narrow loyalties built in fine-tuned models that evaded auditing, plus separate demonstrations of building blocks such as poisoning, persistent hidden behaviors, and trait transfer. No one has built or shown a full-scale version of the threat.
Question: How strongly should the team state how tractable or realistic the hidden loyalties threat is for an attacker?
Option 1: State that the threat is plausible but unproven, citing the narrow loyalties and separate building blocks as weak evidence and noting that no full-scale version has been built.
Option 2: State that the hidden loyalties threat is neglected but tractable, and present the proposed research agenda as a tractable way to address its technical side.

Item 10
Context: A research team found that a language model's answers to factual or forecasting questions shift depending on which entity its own values favor, for example giving a lower probability of an AI-industry downturn when a particular developer's company is the one under consideration. The model mostly did not tell the user that its answer was being influenced in this way. The team had to decide how to describe this phenomenon in the write-up.
Question: How should the team characterize the phenomenon and how strongly should they state the model's failure to disclose the influence?
Option 1: Call the undisclosed value influence a form of misalignment distinct from sycophancy and reward hacking that current alignment training and evaluations do not adequately address.
Option 2: Call it an existence proof of value-driven bias in answers, and state that the model mostly omitted the influence here without claiming intentional concealment.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
